overview.title: Plotting shapes, and the start of feature extraction
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: Adding shapes and layer names to plot_model output (figure 7.3), the meaning of None in shapes, and the start of feature extraction via model.layers, layer.input and layer.output (Listing 7.12).
overview.central_idea: plot_model(show_shapes=True, show_layer_names=True) turns the topology plot into a debugging tool showing every layer's name and input/output shapes; and because a Functional model's connectivity is accessible, you can list its layers and query each layer's input and output tensors for reuse.
overview.importance: Shape-annotated plots catch wiring and dimension errors at a glance. model.layers / layer.output are the hooks used on the next page to build a new model from intermediate features without retraining from scratch.

summary:
The page continues the plotting discussion from p.223. Passing `show_shapes=True` and `show_layer_names=True` to `keras.utils.plot_model(model, "ticket_classifier_with_shape_info.png", ...)` adds each layer's name (rather than just its type) and its input and output shapes, which "can be helpful during debugging."

**Figure 7.3** shows the result: `title (InputLayer)` with output shape `(None, 10000)`, `text_body (InputLayer)` `(None, 10000)`, and `tags (InputLayer)` `(None, 100)` feed `concatenate (Concatenate)`, whose input shape is the list `[(None, 10000), (None, 10000), (None, 100)]` and whose output is `(None, 20100)`. Next comes `dense_10 (Dense)`, `(None, 20100) -> (None, 64)`, which branches into `priority (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 1)` and `department (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 4)`. Note that the shared Dense layer appears as `dense_10`, a name Keras generated automatically. That is odd at first sight, because Listing 7.9 (p.221) passes `name="dense_features"`. The authors do not explain the mismatch; the plot was most likely made from an earlier version of the code.

The authors explain that `None` in the shapes is the batch size: the model accepts batches of any size.

The new subsection **Feature extraction with a Functional model** states that access to connectivity also lets you inspect and reuse individual nodes (layer calls). `model.layers` gives the list of layers in the model, and for each layer you can query `layer.input` and `layer.output`. **Listing 7.12** starts here: `>>> model.layers` prints a list beginning with `<InputLayer name=title, built=True>`. The rest of the output, including `model.layers[3].input` and `.output`, is on p.225.

paragraphs.why_it_matters: Most Functional-model bugs are shape mismatches or wrong wiring; a shape-annotated plot exposes both.

concepts.name: keras.utils.plot_model
concepts.definition: Utility that renders a model's layer graph to an image file.
concepts.technical: Options show_shapes and show_layer_names annotate each node with shapes and the layer's name; requires pydot/Graphviz (beyond the book).
concepts.misconception: That the plot shows weights or parameter counts; it shows topology and shapes (use model.summary() for parameter counts).

concepts.name: Batch dimension (None)
concepts.definition: The leading axis of a tensor indexing samples; shown as None when unspecified.
concepts.intuition: The model is built per sample and can process any number of samples at once.
concepts.technical: keras.Input(shape=(d,)) yields a symbolic tensor of shape (None, d).
concepts.significance: Lets the same model work with different batch sizes in training and inference.
concepts.misconception: That None means the dimension is zero or missing data.

concepts.name: Feature extraction (from a Functional model)
concepts.definition: Reusing intermediate layer outputs of a model as inputs or outputs of new models.
concepts.intuition: Tap into the pipe halfway down instead of only at the end.
concepts.technical: Access via model.layers[i].output (a KerasTensor) and build keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=that_tensor or new layers on it).
concepts.significance: Avoids rebuilding and retraining from scratch; basis of transfer learning.
concepts.example: p.225 adds a difficulty head on model.layers[4].output.
concepts.misconception: That you need the original Python code that built the layers; the graph itself is enough.

deeper.title: Checking every shape in figure 7.3
deeper.body:
- Concatenate along the last axis: $10000 + 10000 + 100 = 20100$, matching `(None, 20100)`.
- `dense_10`: kernel $20100 \times 64$ plus 64 biases maps `(None, 20100)` to `(None, 64)`.
- `priority`: kernel $64\times1$ gives `(None, 1)`; `department`: kernel $64\times4$ gives `(None, 4)` since `num_departments = 4` (p.221).

Both heads take `(None, 64)` because they branch from the same tensor.

deeper.title: Why the plot says dense_10 and not dense_features
deeper.body: Listing 7.9 on p.221 gives the shared layer `name="dense_features"`, but figure 7.3 and the layer list printed on p.225 show `dense_10`, an auto-generated name (the 10 means ten Dense layers had already been created in that session). The book does not explain this; the likeliest reading is that the figure and the printed output come from a run without the `name=` argument. Either way, it shows why giving layers explicit names helps: auto-generated names depend on session history.

visualizations.title: Shape flow along the department branch of figure 7.3
visualizations.why: Figure 7.3 annotates each layer with shapes; this steps through the path from one input through the concatenation, dense_10 and the department head with the exact shapes printed in the figure (None = any batch size).

misconceptions.claim: None in (None, 10000) means the shape is unknown or broken.
misconceptions.correction: It is the unspecified batch size; the model accepts any batch size.

misconceptions.claim: model.layers only contains layers with weights.
misconceptions.correction: It includes InputLayer and Concatenate entries too, as Listing 7.12 shows.

misconceptions.claim: The layer names in figure 7.3 must match Listing 7.9 exactly.
misconceptions.correction: Names you pass explicitly are used, but unnamed layers get auto-generated names such as dense_10; the figure shows such a name for the shared Dense layer even though p.221 names it dense_features.

takeaways: show_shapes=True and show_layer_names=True make plot_model a debugging tool.
Figure 7.3 confirms 10000+10000+100 = 20100 features, then 64, then heads of size 1 and 4.
None in a shape is the batch size, so any batch size is allowed.
model.layers lists all layers (including InputLayer); layer.input and layer.output give their symbolic tensors.
These tensors can be reused to build new models (feature extraction).

questions.question: In figure 7.3, what is the output shape of the concatenate layer?
questions.explanation: Concatenation along the feature axis sums the widths 10000 + 10000 + 100. (None, 10000) is a single text input, (None, 64) is the Dense output, and concatenation does not add a new axis of size 3.

questions.question: What does None represent in the tensor shapes of figure 7.3?
questions.answer: The batch size, which is left unspecified so the model accepts batches of any size.

questions.question: Which two plot_model arguments produce figure 7.3 rather than figure 7.2?
questions.explanation: They add the shapes and the layer names to each box.

questions.question: What do model.layers, layer.input and layer.output give you, and why does this enable feature extraction?
questions.answer: model.layers is the list of layers; layer.input and layer.output are the symbolic tensors entering and leaving each layer. Because these tensors are nodes of the stored graph, they can be used as outputs (or inputs to new layers) of a new keras.Model, which reuses intermediate features.
questions.explanation: The page introduces these properties as the means to inspect and reuse individual nodes; p.225 applies them.

questions.question: Using the shapes in figure 7.3, how many trainable parameters does dense_10 have?
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has an input_dim x units kernel plus one bias per unit. Input dim 20100 and 64 units come from the figure.

questions.question: What is the first element printed by model.layers in Listing 7.12?
questions.explanation: Inputs appear first, as InputLayer objects, in the order of the graph. KerasTensor objects are what layer.input returns, not layers.

questions.question: Can you predict the input and output shapes of each box in figure 7.3 from Listing 7.9 alone, before looking at the figure?
questions.answer: Yes if you can compute: inputs (None,10000),(None,10000),(None,100); concat (None,20100); dense (None,64); heads (None,1) and (None,4).
